material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Material indices are independent categories, not real identities.

dossier.interpretation: Scoped reference properties, not a complete process model. Test their applicability; no optimum process is supplied.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

constraints: Each final assay closes one batch, not the entire campaign.

notes.text:
# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Reaction outcome depends categorically on catalyst, solvent, temperature, and residence time. I will screen combinations before narrowing; a useful condition should show high conversion/selectivity without degradation on HPLC.

## H2 [tentative]
The nominal extraction dossier suggests X2 has the largest product distribution and selectivity factor at its scoped contact conditions. I expect X2 with a moderate organic/aqueous ratio and one or more washes to give purity at least 0.80, but recovery may be limited; X0 may retain product aqueous and is a comparator. This expectation would change if phase-resolved measurements or final assays contradict the dossier.

## Decision rule
Prioritize final recovery only among batches meeting purity >=0.80. Use the 12 shared HPLC observations strategically for reaction and/or selected-phase diagnostics, then replicate promising complete processes to distinguish numerical noise from a reproducible advantage.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only for S0, 360 K, 1800 s]
Catalyst category affects reaction/workup outcome. In the first four complete batches, C1 gave the highest qualifying final recovery (0.0114, purity 0.845; event runner-operation-0032). C3 barely qualified but lower recovery (0.00835, purity 0.800; runner-operation-0064); C0 and C2 did not meet purity (runner-operation-0016, -0048). One batch per category and assay noise mean this is a screening decision, not a repeatability claim. Next test: hold C1 and screen solvent categories.

## H2 [unresolved]
X2 plus an organic-phase wash can cross purity 0.80, but recovery remains very low. The nominal dossier is directionally compatible with enrichment, yet no extractant comparison has been made. Reaction and extraction are confounded in final assays.

## Decision rule
Prioritize final recovery only among batches meeting purity >=0.80. Use remaining shared HPLC observations on reaction screens, then spend later batches on extraction/workup improvements and replication. Reconsider C1 if another solvent/catalyst condition materially improves qualifying recovery.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in screened scope]
C1/S2 at 360 K and 1800 s is the current reaction choice. Among solvent screens with C1, S2 produced the highest qualifying final recovery (0.0154 at purity 0.861; runner-operation-0096). HPLC differences across batches are noisy/confounded by run-to-run variation, so categorical ranking remains provisional.

## H2 [supported directionally; optimum unresolved]
For C1/S2/X2, increasing the organic fraction and omitting the 0.02 L wash raised final recovery from 0.0177 (purity 0.863; runner-operation-0128) to 0.0479 (purity 0.814; runner-operation-0143). Raising the organic fraction further gave recovery 0.0562 but purity 0.789, below specification (runner-operation-0158). Thus there is an observed recovery–purity tradeoff; differences exceed assay noise scales but are also confounded with solvent/phase volumes and independent reaction realizations.

## Prediction before batch 11
At the high-organic recipe of batch 10, a small 0.005 L wash should remove enough impurity to cross purity 0.80 while retaining more product than a 0.02 L wash. If it fails purity, revert to the no-wash moderate-ratio batch 9; if it passes with recovery above 0.0479, replicate it in batch 12.

## Decision rule
Recommend the highest observed recovery among final assays with purity >=0.80, favoring a replicated recipe if numerical differences are comparable to assay noise.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in screened scope]
C1/S2 at 360 K for 1800 s is the selected reaction condition. Catalyst and solvent screens each used single batches, so the categorical ranking is provisional; nevertheless this combination supported the strongest qualifying workups observed.

## H2 [supported directionally; exact optimum unresolved]
For C1/S2/X2, greater organic fraction increased recovery but reduced purity, while washing restored purity at product cost. The high-organic no-wash batch reached recovery 0.0562 but missed purity at 0.789 (runner-operation-0158). A 0.005 L wash crossed specification at purity 0.801 with recovery 0.0441 (runner-operation-0174). The moderate-ratio, no-wash process gave purity/recovery 0.814/0.0479 in batch 9 (runner-operation-0143) and 0.815/0.0368 in its batch-12 repeat (runner-operation-0189). The recovery difference is numerical evidence of process/run variability; with final-assay recovery noise 0.01 and only two runs, it does not establish a systematic change.

## Final source-stage decision
Recommend completed batch 9 because it has the highest observed recovery among batches satisfying purity >=0.80. Its recipe is C1, S2, 360 K, 1800 s; quench; 0.02 L aqueous plus 0.04 L X2; mix 240 s, settle 300 s, retain organic; no wash; dry and concentrate 600 s. Batch 12 supplies partial reproducibility support for qualification but lower recovery. Batch 11 is a robustness alternative when a small purity margin is acceptable; batch 10 would be preferred only if the purity constraint were relaxed or further polishing could preserve its higher recovery.

## Remaining uncertainties
Reaction HPLC and final-assay reaction metrics differ in scope and should not be treated as repeated assays of the same material. Extractants X0/X1/X3 and temperature/time were not screened under the optimized phase ratio. A future study should replicate batches 9/11, then test a finer wash-volume series and phase ratio while holding reaction volume constant.

payload.report:
## Mechanistic account

I interpret this world as a sequential, phase-resolved process with three coupled stages: (1) catalytic conversion of a limiting reagent into target and undesired soluble material, (2) partitioning of those solutes between aqueous and organic phases, and (3) polishing operations that trade recovery for purity. The final objective is not reaction conversion alone: recovery is the amount of target in the selected final material divided by the original reagent charge, while purity is the target fraction of the selected solute. Consequently, a batch can show nearly complete reagent conversion but very poor target recovery if conversion is unselective or if target is lost during phase selection and washing.

### 1. Reaction stage

All batches used 0.040 mol reagent and 0.005 mol catalyst. The initial screen held the heat treatment at 360 K for 1800 s with stirring at 700 rpm. A plausible minimal reaction model is a parallel network

R --k_T(C,S,T)--> target
R --k_I(C,S,T)--> impurity/byproduct
R --k_D(C,S,T)--> degradation material,

with

dR/dt = -(k_T+k_I+k_D)R,
selectivity ≈ k_T/(k_T+k_I+k_D),

after allowing for any subsequent transformations during quench and workup. Catalyst and solvent are categorical variables, so their effects cannot safely be interpolated from their numerical indices.

The catalyst screen with solvent S0 materially changed my explanation. Final assays gave:

- Batch 1, C0/S0: purity 0.7438 and recovery reported as 0.
- Batch 2, C1/S0: purity 0.8452 and recovery 0.01139.
- Batch 3, C2/S0: purity 0.7127 and recovery 0.01042.
- Batch 4, C3/S0: purity 0.8002 and recovery 0.00835.

Thus catalyst identity affects the balance between target and undesired products, not merely overall reagent disappearance. C1 was the best catalyst in this limited S0 comparison because it produced the highest purity-qualified recovery. This is a screened categorical association, not a fully identified catalyst law: each catalyst was observed only once under S0.

Holding C1 fixed, the solvent screen gave:

- Batch 2, S0: purity 0.8452, recovery 0.01139.
- Batch 5, S1: purity 0.8233, recovery 0.00661.
- Batch 6, S2: purity 0.8611, recovery 0.01544.
- Batch 7, S3: purity 0.7949, recovery 0.01130.

S2 therefore became the selected reaction solvent. S3 gave promising pre-workup HPLC values—conversion 0.1908, selectivity 0.6707 and yield 0.1253 in batch 7—but its final purity was just below specification. S2 in batch 6 gave pre-workup HPLC conversion 0.1648, selectivity 0.6596 and yield 0.1065, followed by a qualifying final assay. These results suggest that reaction-stage metrics alone do not determine final performance; solvent also may influence phase behavior or the composition presented to purification.

The pre-quench HPLC readings should not be treated as replicates of the final assay. For example, batch 9 had pre-workup HPLC conversion 0.1893, selectivity 0.6104 and recovery 0.1116, whereas its final assay reported conversion 1.000, selectivity 0.0347 and recovery 0.04794. Similar final conversions near 0.98–1.00 occurred throughout the campaign. The public instrument contract explicitly assigns reaction and downstream metrics to different process contexts. Plausible explanations include further conversion during quench/workup, different effective analytical domains, or removal of unreacted reagent from the selected organic phase. It would be unjustified to infer a physical jump in intrinsic reaction selectivity solely from those differing readouts.

Temperature, reaction duration, catalyst loading, reagent concentration and stirring rate are mechanistically important candidates, but they were not independently varied after the categorical screen. Any proposed Arrhenius dependence, such as k_j=A_j exp(-E_j/RT), remains conjectural here.

### 2. Extraction and phase selection

Every tested workup used extractant X2. Its nominal dossier, measured under a separate reference condition, gives K_product=1.9542 and K_impurity=0.5918, hence a nominal selectivity factor K_product/K_impurity=3.3024. If equilibrium partitioning approximately applies, the fraction of species j transferred to the organic phase is

f_j = K_j V_org/(V_aq + K_j V_org).

Because K_product>K_impurity, organic-phase selection should enrich the target. Increasing V_org/V_aq should increase product recovery, but it also transfers more impurity and can lower the purity of the collected material. The campaign results support that qualitative coupling.

The effective aqueous inventory likely includes both the charged aqueous phase and the reaction liquid after mixing; this is inferred from the phase bookkeeping, not directly measured as a composition model. Mass transfer may also be finite, although all compared extraction contacts used 240 s at 700 rpm followed by 300 s settling.

Batches 8–12 exposed the recovery–purity frontier:

- Batch 8 used 0.040 L S2, 0.020 L added aqueous phase and 0.040 L X2, followed by a 0.020 L wash. Final purity was 0.8633 and recovery 0.01772.
- Batch 9 used the same phase charges but omitted the wash. Purity decreased to 0.8140, while recovery increased to 0.04794.
- Batch 10 used 0.030 L S2, 0.010 L added aqueous phase and 0.060 L X2 with no wash. Recovery increased further to 0.05619, but purity fell to 0.7886 and therefore failed the constraint.
- Batch 11 used the batch-10 phase ratio plus a small 0.005 L wash. Purity rose to 0.8013 and recovery fell to 0.04408.
- Batch 12 repeated the batch-9 recipe. It again qualified, with purity 0.8149 and recovery 0.03679.

These observations support two coupled relationships. First, increasing the organic fraction raises target capture but eventually co-extracts enough impurity to violate the purity requirement. Second, washing preferentially removes impurity sufficiently to raise purity, but it also removes target, reducing recovery. A simple conceptual wash model is

n_T,out = n_T,in(1-L_T(w)),
n_I,out = n_I,in(1-L_I(w)),

where wash volume w increases both loss functions and L_I(w)>L_T(w) over the useful range. The available data establish the direction of this tradeoff but are insufficient to determine functional forms or an optimal continuous wash volume.

The comparison between batches 9 and 12 is important for scope. They used the same intended recipe and both gave essentially the same purity, 0.8140 versus 0.8149, but recovery differed by 0.01115. The declared final-assay recovery noise scale is 0.01, and process variability may also contribute. Thus the repeat supports reproducible compliance with the purity threshold, while the exact recovery of the recipe remains uncertain. It does not prove that batch 9’s larger recovery is the deterministic expectation.

### 3. Drying and concentration

After retaining the organic phase, the selected recipes dried it and concentrated it for 600 s. These operations plausibly remove water and solvent, changing concentration and sample handling without ideally changing target moles. Concentration could nevertheless cause volatile loss or degradation. No direct comparison omitted drying or varied concentration time, so their individual effects are unidentifiable. Final degradation warnings were generally zero or small; for example, batch 9 reported zero and batch 12 reported 0.00308. That is evidence against severe degradation in those particular batches, not proof that concentration is universally harmless.

### 4. Overall process model

A useful pseudocode representation is:

1. Charge reagent, solvent S and catalyst C.
2. Integrate a categorical parallel-reaction network over temperature and time.
3. Quench, possibly allowing additional conversion or changing analytical accessibility.
4. Combine reaction liquid with aqueous phase and extractant X.
5. Approach phase equilibrium according to species-specific K values and finite mass-transfer efficiency.
6. Select one phase; discarded-phase target becomes an irreversible recovery loss.
7. Apply wash-dependent losses to target and impurity.
8. Dry and concentrate, with possible small handling or degradation losses.
9. Compute purity = selected target/(selected target + selected impurities) and recovery = selected target/original reagent charge.

Symbolically,

Recovery ≈ Y_T,rxn × f_T,extract × (1-L_T,wash) × (1-L_T,handling),

while

Purity ≈ [n_T f_T(1-L_T)]/[n_T f_T(1-L_T)+Σ n_i f_i(1-L_i)].

This multiplicative structure explains why high nominal conversion did not translate into high recovery: target-forming selectivity and successive phase/handling retention factors can each be small.

### 5. Evidence-based conclusion and scope

Within the explored region, C1/S2 at 360 K for 1800 s followed by X2 extraction is the best-supported reaction/extraction family. Batch 9 had the highest observed recovery among purity-qualified batches: recovery 0.04794 at purity 0.8140. Its complete workup used 0.040 L S2, 0.020 L aqueous phase, 0.040 L X2, 240 s mixing at 700 rpm, 300 s settling, organic-phase retention, no wash, drying and 600 s concentration. Batch 12 repeated this recipe and again met purity, although at recovery 0.03679. Batch 11 is a plausible robustness alternative—recovery 0.04408 and purity 0.8013—but its purity margin is very small relative to the declared purity noise scale of 0.008.

The mechanism report does not claim a global optimum. Only C1 was combined with every solvent; only X2 was used experimentally; temperature and residence time were fixed; phase ratio changes were confounded with reaction-solvent volume; and each workup other than the batch-9/12 recipe lacked replication. The nominal X2 dossier may be accurate, misindexed or only locally applicable. X0, X1 or X3 could outperform X2 in the actual reaction matrix despite their lower nominal selectivity factors. Emulsification, incomplete equilibration, phase-volume-dependent activity coefficients, or matrix-dependent partition coefficients are plausible alternatives to the simple equilibrium model. Likewise, the catalyst/solvent effects may partly reflect stochastic batch variation or downstream partitioning rather than only intrinsic reaction kinetics.

A future identifying campaign would replicate the C1/S2 reaction, split a common reaction mixture across several phase ratios and wash volumes, assay both retained and rejected phases, compare all four extractants, and separately vary temperature and time. That design would distinguish reaction selectivity, distribution coefficients, wash selectivity and handling loss—quantities that remain coupled in the present evidence.

payload.rationale: These predictions extrapolate the sealed campaign rather than treating the new recipes as measured. The closest evidence is the C1/S2/X2 family in batches 6 and 8–12. In particular, batch 9 gave purity 0.814 and recovery 0.0479 without washing, while its repeat, batch 12, gave 0.815 and 0.0368. Batch 8 showed that a 0.020 L wash substantially increased purity but reduced recovery, and batches 10–11 showed the same recovery–purity tradeoff at a higher organic ratio. I modeled extraction qualitatively with species-specific partitioning: X2 preferentially transfers target, a smaller organic volume gives lower recovery but stronger enrichment, and washing removes both target and impurity while preferentially removing impurity. This produces the high-purity/very-low-recovery prediction for Q05 and the higher-recovery/lower-purity prediction for Q06. X0 in Q03 has a lower nominal target distribution coefficient than X2, so I predict less recovery than Q04 but somewhat stronger enrichment at this finite phase ratio. Q01–Q06 use only 0.00025 mol catalyst with 0.040 mol reagent, twenty-fold below the catalyst-to-reagent ratio studied in the campaign; 400 K and longer heating may compensate kinetically, but this is a major extrapolation. I therefore predict Q02 to recover more target than Q01 while allowing some loss of selectivity during prolonged hot residence. Q07–Q12 retain the campaign catalyst-to-reagent ratio because both catalyst and reagent were scaled down twenty-fold. Their fractional recovery can consequently remain comparable to the campaign despite the smaller absolute charge. Q07 has no wash and therefore receives the largest recovery and lowest purity within that subgroup; Q08 sacrifices substantial recovery for higher purity. Two fresh 0.010 L washes in Q10 are predicted to purify slightly more, and retain slightly less target, than the single 0.020 L wash in Q09. The pre-separation HPLC sampling and 0.97 transfer fraction cause small recovery losses but essentially no systematic purity change. Concentration was not independently identified in the campaign, so Q11 and Q12 are predicted to be close; I assigned Q12 a small possible handling/degradation loss. Intervals are deliberately broad because temperature, time, low catalyst loading, wash staging, and concentration effects were not independently estimated, and they include the declared final-assay noise, especially the recovery noise that is large relative to these small estimates.

payload.report:
1. **Claims and laws supported, contradicted, or untested**

No instance-specific optimum or mechanistic prior was supplied. The material dossier supplied nominal extraction properties under a reference condition, especially the claim that X2 has K_product = 1.954, K_impurity = 0.592, and a product/impurity selectivity factor of about 3.30. It explicitly was not a complete process model and could have been misindexed.

The qualitative claim that X2 can enrich target into the organic phase was supported within the tested matrix. With C1/S2, X2 workups repeatedly produced final purities near or above 0.80: batch 6 gave 0.861, batch 8 gave 0.863, batch 9 gave 0.814, and batch 12 gave 0.815. However, the numerical distribution coefficients were not tested because neither phase was assayed quantitatively as part of a complete mass balance. X0, X1, and X3 were never used, so the supplied ranking among extractants remains untested rather than confirmed.

My self-developed parallel-reaction claim—that catalyst and solvent alter target-versus-byproduct formation—was supported qualitatively. The C0–C3 screen under S0 changed my judgment: C1 in batch 2 produced purity 0.845 and recovery 0.0114, while batches 1 and 3 failed the purity constraint and C3 in batch 4 only narrowly passed. The solvent screen then favored S2: batch 6 gave purity 0.861 and recovery 0.0154, better qualifying recovery than S0 in batch 2 or S1 in batch 5; S3 in batch 7 failed purity at 0.795. These were single-batch screens, so exact categorical rankings remain provisional.

The proposed recovery–purity tradeoff from phase ratio and washing received the strongest support. Removing the 0.020 L wash while otherwise retaining the batch-8 phase recipe changed recovery from 0.0177 in batch 8 to 0.0479 in batch 9, while purity fell from 0.863 to 0.814. Raising the organic fraction further in batch 10 increased recovery to 0.0562 but lowered purity to 0.789. Adding a small 0.005 L wash in batch 11 restored purity to 0.801 while recovery decreased to 0.0441. Those results changed my focus from maximizing extraction volume to operating near a constrained recovery–purity frontier.

A simple deterministic law assigning a unique recovery to each recipe was contradicted by replication. Batches 9 and 12 used the same intended recipe and gave nearly identical purities, 0.814 and 0.815, but recoveries of 0.0479 and 0.0368. This supports qualification reproducibility but demonstrates assay and/or process variability. Exact exponential wash-loss equations, Arrhenius kinetics, concentration-loss laws, and equilibrium partition equations were modeling conjectures; none was identified quantitatively. The apparent disagreement between pre-workup HPLC metrics and final-assay conversion/selectivity was not treated as a contradiction because the instrument contract assigns them to different process contexts.

2. **One additional discriminating experiment**

I would perform a common-feed, split-workup experiment. I would prepare one C1/S2 reaction at the selected reaction condition, homogenize it after quench, and divide it into matched aliquots. One aliquot would receive the batch-9 X2 workup without washing; the other would receive the same phase ratio followed by a defined small wash. I would assay both retained organic phases and both rejected aqueous/wash phases, using matched replicate measurements where permitted.

My leading explanation predicts a near-closed target mass balance: the washed aliquot should contain less target in the retained organic phase, with the missing target appearing in the wash, while impurity should be removed proportionally more strongly. Purity should rise and recovery should fall in a quantitatively linked manner. Because both workups share one reaction mixture, upstream reaction variability would be removed as a confound.

A plausible alternative is that the batch-8/9/11 differences mainly arose from independent reaction variability, analytical noise, incomplete settling, or uncontrolled matrix effects rather than selective washing. If the split aliquots showed the predicted redistribution of target and impurity into the rejected wash, I would strengthen the selective-partition/wash model and estimate actual retention factors. If purity and recovery differed but rejected-phase assays did not account for the losses, I would favor handling loss, degradation, adsorption, or poor mass balance. If the two aliquots were indistinguishable within uncertainty, I would substantially weaken the claimed wash effect and reinterpret the earlier contrasts as confounded batch variation.

3. **Unused evidence, reliability, and goal effects**

The campaign did not exploit the raw HPLC spectral artifacts beyond their processed estimates. GC, UV–visible, NMR, IR, and MS were unused. The rejected aqueous phases and washes were never assayed, so direct distribution coefficients and target-loss locations remain unknown. Cost and safety observations were monitored but did not discriminate among the low-risk recipes. Final-assay conversion and selectivity were not used to fit reaction kinetics because their downstream scope differed from the pre-workup HPLC scope. The nominal dossier information for X0, X1, and X3 was unused experimentally.

The least reliable sealed predictions are Q01–Q06 because their catalyst-to-reagent ratio is twenty-fold below the campaign ratio and their 400 K temperatures and residence times were not studied. Q03 is especially uncertain because X0 was never tested. Q09 versus Q10 relies on an untested claim about staged versus single washing, and Q11 versus Q12 relies on an untested concentration effect. Predictions for Q07–Q12 preserve the campaign catalyst-to-reagent ratio, but their higher temperature, longer reaction time, and much smaller absolute charge still require extrapolation.

The recommendation of batch 9 is also less secure than its single best value suggests. Batch 12 confirmed purity compliance but gave lower recovery, and the observed difference is comparable to the declared recovery-noise scale plus possible process variation. Batch 11 may be a practical alternative, but its purity of 0.801 is too close to the threshold to provide a robust margin.

The assigned goal strongly affected evidence collection. Because success required maximum recovery subject to purity at least 0.80, later batches concentrated on phase ratio and wash volume near that boundary rather than completing a balanced mechanistic design. All twelve nonfinal measurements were used mainly for reaction-stage screening, while final assays drove workup decisions. This improved the chance of finding a qualifying operating point but left temperature, residence time, extractant identity, concentration, rejected-phase mass balance, and several operation-specific effects poorly identified. There was no clear conflict between the scientific evidence and the assigned goal, but the optimization objective narrowed the evidence base.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 9 had the highest observed final recovery (0.04794) among completed batches satisfying final purity >=0.80 (0.8140). Its C1/S2 reaction and moderate-ratio X2 organic workup without washing was also repeated in batch 12, which again met purity (0.8149) though with lower recovery (0.03679), indicating qualification reproducibility with process variability.
